title: ropeway:handbook-title-52
text: A ropeway is a machine on your mechanical network, like a quern or a helve hammer. The drive turns the haul rope, the haul rope pulls the cabin, and the cabin runs at whatever speed the network is turning. Nothing is stored and nothing is banked: a bigger drive is a faster cabin, and no drive is a cabin that waits. Two of your towers are stations There is no block you stand beside the line to drive it. A line is driven by one of its own towers, built on a drive station footing instead of a plain pylon footing, and it is kept taut by another one built on a tension station footing. A station is the same sixteen cells in the same footprint with the same five-wide archway - one leg of it is machinery instead of posts, and half its crossarm is a shaft run instead of braces. Decide which two towers before you build them. 1. Place a drive station footing at the end nearest your mill, facing down the line, and right-click it. The overlay lights all fifteen cells. Build the plain side as usual - four posts of your own material, three ropeway braces - then a bullwheel in the middle of the crossarm instead of the pylon head, and then the machine side: two lay shafts, a drive head on the crossarm end, three drive shafts down the leg, and a drive housing on the ground at its foot. The panel counts the fifteen cells it is short of and goes green when the last one lands - the footing you are reading is the sixteenth block of the tower and is never in that count. 2. Run the mill in. An angled gear at the hub, wooden axles straight down the outside of the drive leg, an angled gear at the bottom, and one level axle into any of the housing's four sides. The drive shafts are the one part of a tower an axle run may lean on, so you build nothing to support that column. The housing's own panel reads out what it is turning at. 3. Place a tension station footing at the far end, facing down the line, and build its fifteen: posts, braces, a bullwheel, two lay shafts, a tension head on the crossarm end, three tension guides down the leg, and a tension weight on the ground. It takes no axle and nothing winds it - it is a counterweight hanging on the rope, and a line will not carry a cabin until one of its towers is a finished tension station. A windmill needs room, and the room decides the height A rotor turns in a flat disc one block thick, standing square to its own axle, and the game will not let you add a sail unless that disc is clear: one clear block for every sail, and one more, counted upward and sideways exactly as much as downward. Nothing behind the rotor along its axle is ever checked, which is why a mill bolts happily to the side of a tower and why the axle run coming out of it never blocks the mill it serves. So a rotor low enough to stand beside a housing on the ground refuses its first sail. Three sails want four clear blocks under the hub; a maxed five-sail wooden rotor wants six. Count the clear blocks rather than a height - the room is what the game checks, and a height is one out or not depending on whether you counted from the grass or from the block resting on it. It is a count of blocks and not of altitude, so a trench under the disc does as well as air: half the clearance can be dug rather than built. So the mill comes down to the intake. The housing is a cell of the station and does not move, so however high the hub ends up, the run is the same shape: an angled gear at the hub, a column of wooden axles down the outside of the drive leg, an angled gear at the bottom, one level axle into the housing. Three sails is about seven blocks of that, a maxed five about nine. Nothing along the rotor's own axle is ever checked for clearance, so the whole descent standing behind the mill never blocks it. And it needs open sky. A rotor that cannot see daylight makes no torque at all, however hard the wind blows and however clear its disc: the game reads the sky light at the hub, and a mill under a roof, a canopy or an overhanging shelf of rock reads dark and simply stands still. That is about cover and not about the hour - a mill in the open turns all night. It is the last remaining way to build the whole drive correctly and get nothing out of it, so if the disc is clear and the weather is good, look up. The maxed metal rotor is the tall one. Ten sails need eleven clear blocks every way, which stands that hub eleven blocks up - the same build as the others, with a column of eleven axles instead of four. The bottom three lean on the drive leg; the rest stand beside open air, so give those a wall or the gear at the foot refuses to place. That is vanilla's rule about unsupported axles, not the ropeway's. The bullwheel is the wheel the station turns Both stations carry one in the middle of the crossarm, in place of the pylon head, and a plain tower does not take one. It is not itself on the mechanical network - no axle enters it - but its hub axle runs out through its two bearings and along the crossarm to the machinery, so the drive is a line you can follow with your eye from the housing on the ground to the wheel in the air. What it does is turn, at the speed your drive is turning, and stop when your drive stops. Both wheels on a line turn together, because they are watching the same rope. A bigger mill is a faster cabin Hauling a cabin is a heavy load - about three querns' worth - and the line's speed is what your drive has left over after carrying it. In good wind, on the level: Two sails - a wooden rotor with two sails will not shift the cabin at all. Three sails - about 1.2 blocks a second, a walking pace. Five sails, a maxed wooden rotor - about 2.2. Ten sails, a maxed metal rotor - about 3.0, a run. Where the mill stands matters as much as how big it is Those speeds are good wind, and good wind is the top of the range rather than the middle of it. Wind also strengthens with height. The same maxed wooden rotor that barely creeps the cabin along - a third of a block a second - down at sea level in ordinary weather will run it at over 1.6 from a ridge eighty blocks up, and a three-sail mill in the valley will often not move it at all. Put the drive high. A ropeway is a mountain machine, and so is the mill that drives it. Water wheels A water wheel does not care what the weather is doing, and it is the one drive that hooks up with nothing to climb and no gears at all: power comes out of both ends of its own axle, at most a block above the water surface, so two or three level axles reach the housing at the foot of the drive leg. Where the terrain allows it, it is the cheapest hookup in the mod. It asks for everything up front instead. A wheel only turns in rapidly flowing water - the white water that generates, rarely, in high mountain streams, and that no player can place or make. Ordinary river water will not move it, however deep or fast it looks. The wheel is iron-age as well: two four-way hubs on an axle to craft the block, and then six stages of construction on the spot in support beams, planks, resin and nails. And it is capped lower than a windmill - whatever the river does, a water wheel cannot run the cabin past about 1.8 blocks a second. Constant, capped and built where the map allows, against faster but at the mercy of the wind and the altitude: that is the whole choice. Gearing and anything else on a vanilla network behave as they do everywhere else. You never have to guess: the drive housing's block info panel reads out what it is turning at, and any footing's reads what the line comes to in blocks a second. If nothing moves, read the footing. It tells you which of the two things is missing - a drive station that is turning, or a finished tension station - and right-clicking a station's footing lights the cells it is still short of. Any tower may be the drive station, and drives add up No particular tower has to be the driven one - build the drive station wherever the terrain suits the mill, wind on a ridge or water in the valley, and the rest of the line is plain towers. If one mill is not enough, build a second drive station as another tower of the same line, on its own axle network. Their speeds pool, so two mills is a visibly faster cabin. It has to be a second network, mind: two stations tapped off the one axle run are the same drive twice over, and they are worse than one - the line reads that drive's speed once, but each housing puts the full haul load on that network, so the cabin ends up slower. And a drive turns the line it is a tower of and no other, so two lines running side by side each want their own drive station however close together they pass. A station's machine leg stands three blocks out from its footing, so two towers built close together can want the same cell - and if they do, one of them simply never finishes: its panel keeps counting the cell it is short of and the overlay reddens it. Move one tower. No station ever shares another one's machinery, however close you build them, so nothing is quietly driving a line it is not a tower of. Intermediate drive stations were real on long ropeways for exactly this reason: driving the haul loop anywhere along its length drives all of it. Climbing costs A climbing cabin is a heavier load than a level one, so the same mill turns slower while it climbs and picks up again on the flat. On a steep line a small mill crawls. That is the machine working rather than a fault - and it is the honest reason to put a bigger rotor on a mountain line. Dead calm Vanilla weather goes still for hours at a time and no windmill of any size makes torque then. The cabin stops where it is and waits, exactly like a quern with nobody turning it, and sets off again by itself when the wind returns. A stopped cabin is not a locked one - but mind where it stopped. Sneak steps you straight out of it wherever it happens to be, and if that is halfway across a span, you step out into the air and take the fall. Ride it out, or pick your moment. A cabin that is moving refuses that same key press until you hold it down - see Building a Line. If you would rather not wait on the weather, drive the line with something that does not depend on it, or build a second drive somewhere the wind reaches when the first one's does not. Back to Aerial Ropeways.
